turns.text: I handed in my notice at Verano this morning. Eleven years on the line and I am going to go make bread instead.
That is a big move. Do you have a space in mind, or is this still the idea stage?

Two spaces. There is 900 square feet on Halvard Street at $3,200 a month, empty, needs everything. And a 400 square foot stall in the Kettle Row market hall for $2,150, but the oven there is shared with a pie guy.
The shared oven is what I would worry about. How much of your production has to come out same morning?
All of it. That is the entire point. I have $46,000 saved and my brother in law will lend me ten more if I ask him nicely.
Then Halvard gives you control but eats the cushion fast. Do you want me to sketch what a build out on 900 empty feet usually swallows?
Not tonight. I mostly wanted to say it out loud to someone who was not going to tell me I am insane.
Signed on Halvard. Five years, two months free while I build out, three percent bumps every year after.
Congratulations. Who is the landlord, and is the free build out period actually in the document?
Denise Okonkwo, she owns the whole block. It is in the lease. The one surprise is that she wants a grease trap even though I am not frying a single thing.
Worth pushing back, though city code sometimes forces it regardless of what you cook. Do you have a name yet?
That is the other thing. I have been going in circles for a month. Third Rise, Halvard Bread Co, or Crumb Theory.
Crumb Theory is the cleverest and the hardest to say twice out loud. Third Rise means something to a baker and nothing to anyone else, which is not a problem.
Third Rise. Done. My wife hates it, which is how I know it is mine.
Oven decision. There is a used Rondelle DK4, four decks, $11,500, coming out of a pizzeria that closed in Ashcroft. Or a new Bellweather S2 at $28,000 with a five year warranty.
What shape is the used one in? Have you seen it fired?
I watched it come up to 260 and hold there for an hour. Stones are chipped on the bottom deck but the elements look newer than the oven does.
Then the real question is what $16,500 of cushion is worth to you in month three, when something else breaks.
That is exactly where I keep landing. Taking the Rondelle.
Bad news is it wants three phase power. Nate Guillory quoted me $6,800 to bring it in from the street.
That is a real number. Worth asking whether the building already has three phase somewhere. Dry cleaners and print shops leave it behind all the time.
Denise did not know. I will dig.
You were right about the three phase. The previous tenant was a dry cleaner and the panel is still sitting behind the drywall in the back corner.
That is the best kind of surprise. What does it do to Nate's number?
$2,700 instead of $6,800. He only has to run it forty feet and set a new disconnect.
So the building handed you back $4,100. What is the health department saying?
The inspector came Tuesday. She wants a mop sink I do not have and a dedicated handwash separate from the three compartment sink. Neither is expensive. Both are inside a wall I already closed up.
Is that a plumber callback or a you job?
It is a me job at eleven at night with a reciprocating saw. Opening slips two weeks either way.
I think I found my baker. Marisol Vega, five years at a wholesale place in Ashcroft doing four hundred loaves a night.
That is serious volume experience. What is she asking?
$24 an hour. I offered $22 plus a cut of the Saturday tips and she looked at me like I had insulted her mother.
Where did you land?
$23 and the tips. Worth every cent of it. She shapes faster than I do and she understands the retarder better than I do.
And the front of the house?
Teddy Ferris, my neighbor's kid. Weekends only. He is nineteen and terrifyingly good with people.
Test bakes all week and the crumb on the country loaf is tight and slightly gummy and I am losing my mind.
What is your hydration, and how long is the bulk?
76 percent, bulk overnight in the retarder at 12 degrees, shape at five, first bake at seven.
The schedule sounds fine. Tight and gummy at 76 with a long cold bulk usually means underdeveloped rather than overfermented.
I pushed to 80 percent and added two more coil folds and it opened right up. Gladys is happy again.
Gladys being the starter, I assume.
Twelve years old. Pia Roldan gave me a jar of her the week I left her kitchen and told me that if it died she would know.
Opening day is February 7th. Soft open on the 5th for the block, free bread, see what breaks.
Sensible. What is still outstanding?
The sign. Oldfield Signs pushed me to February 20th because their router is down and the part is coming from overseas.
Two weeks open with no sign is survivable if the smell does its job. Any interim plan?
I painted a sheet of plywood black and did the name across it in white house paint. It honestly looks better than the sign will.
Keep it afterward. What else is on the list?
Insurance binder, a card reader, and six hundred pounds of flour landing on the 3rd. Sleep is not on the list.
We opened. Sold out at 10:40 on Saturday, 220 loaves out the door.
That is a real opening. What went wrong, since something always does?
The card reader dropped for forty minutes right in the middle of the rush. I wrote orders on receipt paper and told people to come back and pay. Eleven of the fourteen did.
That is a better return rate than most people would guess.
The cash box had $1,340 in it at close, which felt enormous until I remembered what flour costs.
What moved and what did not?
The seeded rye. I called it the Halvard Rye and it went first every single day. The olive fougasse died on the shelf, nine unsold on Saturday alone.
First month is closed out. $31,400 in revenue, about eight thousand over what I put in the plan.
Strong first month. Where is the pressure?
Flour. The Bergstrom high extraction went from $22.50 a bag to $27.80 and my miller says it is not coming back down this year.
On fifty pound bags, at your volume, that is meaningful. Is there a lever on the retail side?
I am not raising a loaf to nine dollars in month two. I would rather find volume.
Marisol also asked for Sundays. I am closing Sunday and Monday both. If I am going to lose a day I would rather lose two and actually rest.
That gives the starter a clean rest and you a real maintenance window.
There is a cafe on Bellamy called Lumen that keeps asking about wholesale. I have been putting them off, but maybe that is the volume.
Lumen is signed. Forty loaves a week at $4.25 wholesale against an $8 retail loaf.
How does that pencil once you count delivery?
It pencils because I am already awake and their back door is nine minutes from mine. It is margin on flour I am already buying.
Fair. What else is moving?
Teddy leaves in May, going back for his associate's. I hired Nour Haddad off a handwritten note she left on the counter, which is the most Third Rise way to get a job.
Noted. How is the equipment holding up?
It is not. The retarder compressor died on a Tuesday night with forty loaves in it. Kestrel Refrigeration had me running by noon for $980 and I lost the whole bake.
June is slower than I expected. Everyone is at the shore and nobody wants a hot oven, theirs or mine.
Is that a demand problem or a habit problem?
Both. So I started Friday pizza night. The decks are already at temperature at four and I am throwing sixty pies between five and eight.
Using the oven for what it was built for. Is it pulling people in?
It is pulling an entirely different crowd. And Colleen Tsai from the Fenmore Weekly came in on a Friday, wrote three hundred words about the rye, and we did thirty percent more for two solid weeks.
Any thought to a second baker, so you can occasionally be somewhere other than the bakery?
I am interviewing a guy named Devesh on Thursday. I have not had a day off since February 7th and my daughter drew a picture of me as an oven.
Third year officially started and I still cannot get boat time. The Loomis lab has the skiff booked Tuesday and Thursday through May.
Is that schedule set by the department, or by whoever asks first?
Whoever asks first, which is the whole problem. My transects at Vasse Inlet have to be sampled on a two week cadence or the growth curve is garbage.
Can Halloway intervene? A note from an advisor tends to move a shared resource calendar faster than a student email does.
Halloway avoids conflict the way other people avoid wasps. I will ask Okoye, who is on my committee for the stats and who has actual elbows.
Who else is on the committee?
Halloway, Okoye, and Ferrante as the external. Ferrante is a plant physiologist and asks the questions nobody else thinks to ask, which I resent and need.
The Renshaw Coastal Fellowship is open. Eighteen thousand dollars for a summer field season, due April 2nd.
What does it actually fund, stipend or field costs?
Both, which is why everyone in the building applies. I need a letter from outside my department and I am going to ask Ferrante.
Do you have a draft of the research statement I can react to?
Not yet. The pitch is transplant density as a lever on eelgrass survival. Three densities, six plots, two seasons of monitoring.
That reads clean. Ask Ferrante this week. External letter writers need three weeks or they get resentful.
I got the Renshaw. The full amount, no cuts.
Congratulations. What does that unlock that you could not do otherwise?
Loggers. I ordered twelve TidePoint 2 temperature loggers at $210 each, which is more than I have spent on anything except my car.
Twelve across six plots?
Two per plot. One at canopy height and one in the sediment. Plus a pooled boat budget so I can stop begging the Loomis lab for Thursdays.
When does planting start?
June 3rd if the weather cooperates. Ruth Kealoha is my field assistant. She is a junior and she can hold her breath much longer than I can.
A storm came through on July 2nd and took plots 4 and 5 apart. Forty percent of the transplants are gone.
Gone as in uprooted, or buried?
Uprooted and scoured. The sediment itself moved. I sat in the boat and did not say anything for about ten minutes.
Is there a version of this where the storm is data rather than damage?
That is what Ruth said, in fewer words. If I treat July 2nd as a disturbance event I have a before and after at three densities, which nobody in this system has.
So the design changed rather than broke.
There is also a green crab problem. They are pulling shoots out at the edges of every plot and I have no way to fence sixty square meters of seafloor.
First pass at survival. 61 percent in the high density plots and 28 percent in the low.
That is a big separation. How much of it survives the storm confound?
That is the question. Okoye says fit it as a mixed model with plot as a random effect and disturbance as a fixed factor, and stop trying to average my way out of it.
Do you have the tooling for that?
Not really. I have been doing everything in one enormous spreadsheet like a coward. I am taking a four day Bayesian workshop in October so I can stop.
Is Okoye willing to read the model before the chapter goes out?
She offered. She also said that if I send her a spreadsheet again she will send it back unopened.
Halloway wants Wen Li as second author on chapter two. Wen is his new postdoc and has not been to the site once.
What did Wen contribute, in Halloway's telling?
Framing. Which means he talked about it in lab meeting twice.
And Ruth?
Ruth was in the water every sampling day for eleven weeks and built half the logger housings herself.
What would you accept, if you had to name it before the meeting?
I said Ruth third and Wen in the acknowledgements. Halloway blinked first, which I did not expect. Ruth is third and Wen is not on it at all.
Estuarine Society abstracts are due December 15th. The meeting is in Corvallis in March.
Are you pitching the density result or the disturbance framing?
The disturbance framing. The density result on its own is a poster and I am tired of standing next to posters.
What is the risk if the committee reads it as a salvage story?
That is exactly the risk. So I am leading with the design and letting the storm show up in the third paragraph like a plot twist.
Do you want me to read the 250 words before you submit?
Tomorrow. Tonight I am going to eat crackers and stare at a wall.
Halloway sent chapter two back. His comment on page one is that it reads like a report and not an argument.
Harsh. Is he wrong?
He is not wrong. I wrote it in the order I did the work instead of the order someone would need in order to believe it.
So restructure around the claim.
Around disturbance. The claim is that density buys resistance and that you only see it once something knocks the system over. Everything else is support for that.
Also, unrelated and not unrelated, Alix got an offer in Halifax. Which is eleven hundred kilometers from every eelgrass bed I have ever touched.
Is that a decision for now or for after the defense?
I do not know yet. That is the honest answer.
Corvallis is done. Twelve minutes, no technical disasters, one question I could not answer.
What was the question?

Sabine Voss asked whether my density effect is really a light attenuation effect, since canopy shading changes the light field at the sediment. I said I would have to check my loggers, which was a polite way of saying I have no light data.
Is there a way to get it?
Voss has it. Two years of light sensors in a system forty kilometers south of mine, and she offered to share if I bring her on the paper. I said yes before she finished the sentence.
And the job question?
Postdoc or an agency job. The agency pays thirty percent more and lets me sleep. The postdoc is the one everyone assumes I want.
Defense is October 9th.
Committee unchanged?
No. Ferrante is on sabbatical in Chile through December, so Amrit Basu is taking the external seat. Basu is a seagrass person, which is better and much scarier.
Better because he will know the system.
Better because he will know when I am hand waving. I am rewriting the chapter three discussion this month with him in mind.
I also applied for the Tidewater Policy Fellowship, which would put me in a management agency for a year starting next February.
And Halifax?
Alix took it. Starts in September. We are going to try the version where I finish first and then we figure it out, which everyone says never works.
Kindergarten registration opens next week and I have been putting this decision off for four months.
What are the options?
Barlow Elementary is our zoned school. Six blocks, fine, boring. Cedarcrest has the Spanish dual language program but it is a lottery and it is a fifteen minute drive.
Is the dual language piece important to you specifically?
My mother spoke Spanish to me until I was seven and then I lost it, and I have been quietly angry about that for thirty years. So yes.
And Junie?
Junie says whatever gets them fed and read to. She is on nights at the hospital pharmacy so mornings are mine either way.
They turn five on March 11th. Ines will walk in and run the place. Mateo will need me to sit in the parking lot for a week.
Mateo had a reaction at a birthday party on Saturday. Hives up his neck and his lips went puffy. We did Benadryl and then the emergency room.
Is he all right now?
He is fine. It was a peanut butter cookie that somebody swore up and down was sunflower butter.
Did they test him?

Dr. Warrick ran it. Peanut specific IgE came back at 14.2 and the skin prick was a nine millimeter wheal, so there is nothing ambiguous about it. Two junior epinephrine pens, one for home and one for school.
Do you want help drafting the school health plan?
Yes. And a one page version I can hand my mother in law that she will actually read.
Cedarcrest called. We were number 14 on the waitlist and enough families moved over the summer that we got in.
That is a real result. Does it change the morning logistics much?
Fifteen minutes each way, twice a day. Which means my day has a hole in it from 8:40 to 2:50 and I have to decide what goes in the hole.
What do you want to go in it?
Work, probably. I was a GIS technician for the county and I have not drawn a paycheck since 2019. Six years is long enough that people look at the resume and squint.
Six years with two children in them is not a gap, but I take your point about how it reads on paper.
Help me write the paragraph that says that without sounding like I am apologizing for it.
The Corolla has officially lost. Two boosters and the dog and a stroller and there is nowhere left for groceries.
Van, then. What are you looking at?
A 2019 Odyssey with 84,000 miles for $21,400, or a 2020 Sienna hybrid with 61,000 for $26,900. The Odyssey is the better deal on paper.
Did either one get a pre purchase inspection?
Ferko did both. He got under the Odyssey and called me over to look at the rear subframe, which had rust coming through in flakes, not film. He said he would not let his sister buy it.
So the Sienna.
Sienna. Paid $26,400 in the end because the inspection report gave me something to point at. Thirty five miles a gallon and there is a vacuum built into the back like it is a spaceship.
Three applications out, one interview so far.
Where?
Rowe and Vance, a survey firm on the west side. GIS tech, mostly parcel work and cleaning up drone imagery. They said $58,000.
How did the six year question go?
The hiring manager asked what I had been doing and I said raising twins, rebuilding a deck, and teaching myself PostGIS at night, in that order, and she laughed and moved on.
What is the other thing you applied for?
The county posts their tech openings in September. That is the one I actually want, because I know the data already and the pension is real.
First day. Ines walked in without looking back and Mateo cried so hard he got the hiccups.
How long did the crying last?
Eleven minutes, according to the teacher, who texted me a photo of him laughing at 9:15. I will owe her forever.
And the allergy plan?
That is the fight. Cedarcrest does a nut free table in the cafeteria, not a nut free building, and the office told me that like it was good news.
Did you push?

I pushed. I got the table plus a wipe down of his classroom tables before his class comes in, and the pen kept in the classroom instead of locked in the nurse's office, which was the part that actually mattered.
I took the Rowe and Vance job. Started on the 13th, four days a week, Monday through Thursday.
How is it?
My hands remember more than my head does. I opened a parcel layer on day two and just knew where the errors would be.
What did four days do to the childcare math?

Junie covers Monday and Tuesday afternoons because she is on nights. Wednesday afternoon is the hole. Priscilla next door takes them from 2:50 until I get home at 5:30 and she will not accept a cent, so we feed her family on Sundays.
And the county job?
It posted and I let it go by. I had been out six years. I was not going to turn down the first real offer to wait on a process that takes four months.
The dishwasher let go on New Year's Eve and put water under the floor in half the kitchen.
What is the insurance saying?
They paid $6,200 on the water damage. Which sounds like a lot until you learn what a plumber costs on a holiday.
Are you repairing or renovating at this point?
It started as a repair and then Junie said if the floor is coming up anyway, and now the cabinets on the sink wall are going too.
Who is doing the work?
Bo Nyquist. He did my neighbor's bathroom. He is slow but he does not lie, which is apparently the trade.
He says three weeks. I have been told three weeks before.
Sixth birthday is Saturday. The trampoline place, twelve kids, and I have to survive it.
What is the cake plan?
Zoya's. They run a dedicated allergen free kitchen and they label everything. Chocolate with the dinosaur on it, plus a second small one so Mateo has one nobody else has breathed on.
How is he doing generally?
Better than I expected. His IgE came down to 6.8 at the January check and the allergist started talking about an oral challenge, maybe next year, in a clinic, with everything ready.
How did that land with you?
I said yes out loud and then sat in the car for a while. The idea of deliberately feeding him a peanut in a room does something to my chest.
The kitchen is done. Five weeks late and $9,800 all in.
So $3,600 past what the insurance covered.
Yes, and about two thousand of that is cabinets we chose to do, so I can only be so annoyed. Bo's work is good. Bo's calendar is a rumor.
What else is moving?
Junie goes to days in July. Which means that for the first time since 2019 we will both be awake at the same time on a weekday.
And work?
They are floating senior tech for me. It is a title and about four thousand dollars and it means I would own the parcel QC process, which is the part I would do for free.
I am in. Kalve Ridge 100k, June 13th. Registration opened at eight and was gone by ten past.
What does the course look like?
5,800 meters of vertical over the whole thing and a twenty hour cutoff. Three real climbs and one stupid one at kilometer 80.
What is your base right now?
Seventy kilometers a week, nothing above four hours. Petter wants me at ninety by February with two vertical sessions a week.
Is Petter coaching you formally or informally?
Formally now. Twelve hundred kroner a month and he writes the week on Sunday nights. Worth it because I cannot be trusted to take an easy day.
Base block is going well. Eighty two kilometers last week and I felt fine on Sunday, which is new.
Any niggles?
Left shin is a bit talkative on the road sections but it settles once I am warm.
Worth mentioning to Petter.
I mentioned it. He said shoes. I have been putting everything long in the Torrent Lyra 3, which is a soft high stack shoe and my main trainer since last spring.
How many kilometers are on that pair?
About six hundred, which is past where I usually rotate them out. I ordered a second pair rather than change anything two weeks before Christmas.
It was not the shoes. Rasmussen scanned it and it is a tibial stress reaction on the left, medial, low grade but real.
What is the prescription?
Four weeks with no running at all. Pool running, bike, and he was very clear that the bike does not count as cross training if I race the intervals.
How are you taking it?
Badly. June 13th is twenty one weeks away and four of them are now gone.
Four weeks in January is the cheapest four weeks you could have lost.
I know that intellectually. Ask me again on Saturday when the group does the Grindal traverse without me.
Started with a physio, Hedda Lindqvist. She does a lot of the ski team, so she is unbothered by me.
What is the program?
Eccentric calf raises, three sets of twenty five, every day. Then a hopping progression once I am pain free on single leg loading for a week.
Did anyone look at the underlying reasons rather than the leg?
Hedda sent me for bloods. Ferritin came back at 18 and vitamin D at 32, both of which she called low enough to matter for bone.
What did she put you on?
Iron every other day with vitamin C, and 2000 units of D through the winter. And she told me my eating window is too narrow around the long days, which was the part I did not want to hear.
Running again. Started at twenty minutes of run walk on grass and I have built to fifty minutes continuous.
Any shin signal?
Nothing. Quiet. I am touching wood as I type.
What does Petter have you doing for the vertical you lost?
Uphill hiking with poles and no downhill until April. For the rocky descents I picked up the Kessel Fell, which is a low stack shoe with a proper lug, so I stop skating on wet rock.
Two very different shoes for two very different jobs.
That is the idea. First two hour run back was the Grindal traverse on Sunday and I cried a bit at the top, which I am blaming on wind.
Fueling block. I have been testing on the long runs and I can hold seventy grams of carbohydrate an hour without any trouble.
What are you using?
Sift drink mix for the bulk of it, plus rice cakes with jam every second hour so my mouth has something to do that is not sweet.
Did you test the upper end?
I tried ninety and it fell apart at hour four. Bloating, then nothing wanted to go down at all. Seventy is my number and I am not being brave about it on race day.
What about crew?
Kare is driving. He takes me at kilometer 42 and again at kilometer 68, which are the only two places crew is allowed on that course.
Bjorka 50k yesterday as the tune up. 6:12, ninth woman, and I was not trying to be ninth.
How did the leg hold?
Nothing at all from the shin. My quads were destroyed by kilometer 35 from the descents, which is a training gap, not an injury.
Anything you would change for June?
Poles. I borrowed a pair for the last climb and they changed the day, so I bought the Skarv carbon Z folding ones on the way home.
Anything that surprised you?
How much time I lost in aid stations. Eleven minutes total across four stops for a race I was trying to run fast. On a 100k that becomes forty.
Two weeks out. Taper started Sunday, volume down to fifty and the intensity stays.
Is everything settled equipment wise?
Almost. The Lyra 3 got discontinued and the replacement fits differently, so I moved to the Verge Trail 2 for the long stuff and I have put sixty kilometers into them to be sure.
That is cutting it fine but it is enough.
Drop bags close on the 10th. Two bags, one at 42 and one at 68, both with socks, a headlamp battery, and food.
What about weather layers?
The forecast is warm so I am packing light. Shell in the pack, nothing heavier.
I did not finish. Pulled myself at kilometer 74.
What happened?

The ridge after 68 turned. Rain came sideways at about eight degrees and I had packed for the forecast, not for the mountain. My insulated jacket was in the bag at 42 because I moved it at the last minute.
Were you near a cutoff?

No, and that is the part people keep getting wrong. The cutoff at Sorhaug was 12:40 and I came through at 12:01. I was inside the clock. I stopped because I could not feel my hands and I was slurring at the marshal.
That sounds like the right call rather than a failure.
It was the right call. It still took me two days before I could say the word hypothermia instead of saying I was fine and made a decision.
Kare drove me home and did not say anything for an hour, which is the nicest thing anyone has done for me.
New plan. Ardal 100k on September 26th. Smaller race, less vertical, and I know the last thirty kilometers of it.
What changes between now and then?
Two things. Every drop bag gets the same fixed list and I do not edit it on the morning. And I carry the insulated layer whatever the forecast says, even if it is a kilo I never use.
And the training?
I joined a Tuesday hill group so the vertical stops being a thing I negotiate with myself. Eight of us, and two of them are much faster than me, which is the point.
How is the leg?
Silent since March. I had a scare in June that I was sure was a fracture and it was the same shin being dramatic after a cold night.
Fourteen years estimating for Cardell Interiors and I am done. Ron takes my numbers, shaves eight percent off them to win the job, then asks me why the crews are behind.
Is this a change jobs situation or a start your own thing situation?
Start my own. I know every builder in this county by their first name and half of them have asked me why I still work for Ron.
What does the money look like if you jump?
Seventy two thousand a year goes to zero. Nineteen thousand in savings. Yvette has her school job and insurance, which is the only reason this is even a conversation.
What does Yvette say?
She says I have been talking about this for six years and she is not going to be the reason I do not. Which is not the same as saying yes.
Gave notice Monday. Ron offered me four thousand more to stay and I laughed before I could stop myself.
What is the setup work?
The LLC is filed. Deewell Surfaces. General liability is eighteen fifty a year through a broker my brother uses, one million per occurrence.
License?
Exam is May 22nd. Business and law plus the trade section. I have been doing this work for twenty years and I still have to sit a test on lien deadlines.
Do you want a study plan for the business and law half?
Yes. That is the half that will get me. I can do takeoffs in my sleep and I cannot tell you what a mechanics lien deadline is in this state.
Passed. 78 out of a hundred, seventy to pass, so no medals but I never have to look at that book again.
Congratulations. What is next on the list?
A truck. My personal truck is not going to haul a thousand pounds of luxury vinyl plank twice a week.
What did you find?
A 2016 Transit 250, 118,000 miles, $17,900 from a plumbing outfit that upgraded their fleet. Clean records, one owner, and the shelving is already in it.
Cash or financed?
Put six down and financed twelve at 8.9, which I hate. But keeping cash in the account is the only thing that lets me say no to a bad job.
First real bid went out and I lost it. Dental office remodel, 4,200 square feet of luxury vinyl plank, full demo of the old tile.
What did you bid?
$38,600. The guy who took it came in at $31,000 and I do not know how he gets there without either eating the demo or paying his guys in sandwiches.
Do you think your number was wrong?
My number was right. My waste factor is at twelve percent and it could be nine on a room that square. That is fifteen hundred dollars, not seven.
So it is a market problem, not a math problem.
It is a first year problem. Nobody hands a new outfit a $38,000 job. I picked up 900 square feet of hardwood refinish for $5,400 out of the same phone call, so the day was not a total loss.
Hired a helper. Dominic, twenty six, four years with a tile crew, wants out of tile.
What are you paying?
$21 an hour. He asked for twenty three and I told him what my first year looks like and he said fine, ask me again in a year.
Cash flow?
Tight. That is the whole story of the month. I opened an account with Halcyon Supply on net 30 terms with a $10,000 credit limit, which buys me a month between buying material and getting paid.
Does the limit cover a typical job?
It covers anything up to about three thousand square feet. Above that I am putting material on a card and praying, which is not a business plan.
I have a problem client and I want to talk it through before I do something stupid.
Go ahead.
Bellview Apartments. Property manager named Sherry Dolan. Eleven units of luxury vinyl plank, $46,000 contract, turn them as tenants move out.
What is going wrong?

She paid the first draw on time. Since then it is a new excuse every Friday. Corporate is reviewing, the portal is down, the regional is on vacation. I have finished seven units and been paid for three.
What are you going to do?
I stopped at unit 7. Pulled my tools out Wednesday and told her the crew comes back when the second draw clears. She said that puts me in breach, which tells me she has done this before.
Bellview is settled, mostly. I filed the lien in November inside the deadline, which is the only thing that book was ever good for.
What did you recover?
They owed $31,000 on the work I finished. I took $28,000 to make it go away rather than spend another six months on it.
What did the process cost you?
Aaron Petty, $2,200 in fees. Plus about three weeks of not sleeping and one very ugly phone call in front of my kid.
Anything changing structurally?

Yes. Forty percent down before material hits the site, draws every three units, and work stops the day a draw is late. No exceptions and no friends rates. I lost two prospects over it in December and I do not care.
I missed a quarterly payroll deposit. Did not know I had missed it until the notice came.
How bad?
$410 penalty plus interest that rounds to nothing. Bad enough to be embarrassing, not bad enough to hurt.
How did it get missed?
Because I was doing payroll out of a spiral notebook and my own memory, like it is 1988.
Fixed how?
Bookkeeper. Lanelle, three hundred a month, she does payroll, the quarterlies, and reconciles the supply account. Best three hundred dollars I spend.
Tunbridge Homes wants me on six spec houses this year. Same package in each, flooring throughout.
What is that worth?
About $96,000 across the year if all six get built, and their draw schedule is written into the contract, which after last winter is most of why I said yes.
Can you staff it?
Not with one helper. I need a second crew, which means Dominic runs one and I run the other and I stop swinging a hammer three days a week.
Is he ready for that?
He is better at layout than I am and he is bad at telling a customer no. I can teach the second thing.
Bought a ride on floor scraper. $6,300 used, and it took a two day demo down to four hours.
That pays for itself quickly at your volume.
Three jobs. And my back gets ten more years out of it, which is not on any spreadsheet.
How is the year running?
$214,000 in revenue through June. Second van bought in May, both crews running four days most weeks.
And the office side?
Yvette took over scheduling on Tuesdays and Thursdays and my callbacks went from three days to same day. She keeps pointing out she has been telling me that since March.
Baram Labs said yes. I can keep my role and work from anywhere in Europe as long as I make the Tuesday planning call.
Congratulations. Have you picked a country?
Portugal. I went for two weeks in April and I have thought about the light every day since, which is not a reason but it is my reason.
What is the visa route?
The D8, the one for remote workers. You have to show income at four times the Portuguese minimum wage and my salary clears it, but the paperwork wants twelve months of statements.
What is the first blocking step?
A tax number. You cannot rent, you cannot open a bank account, you cannot do anything without one, and you cannot get one easily from outside the country.
I am making a list. The list already has nineteen things on it and I have not booked a flight.
Tax number done. I used a lawyer in Lisbon, Rui Marques, who acted as my fiscal representative because I am not resident yet.
What did that cost?
180 euros including his first year as representative. There are services that charge less but they are all forms in a website and I wanted a person with a name.
Banking next?
I opened a digital account first because a real Portuguese bank wants you standing in the branch. The digital one is enough for the rent deposit and the visa file.
How is the list going?
Thirty one items now. It grows faster than I close it. My mother has started asking how long the whole thing takes as a way of asking me not to go.
Visa appointment is booked for September 30th in Seoul.
What has to be in the folder?
Criminal record certificate with an apostille, twelve months of bank statements, the employment contract, proof of accommodation, and health insurance.
What counts as proof of accommodation before you have moved?
A lease of at least twelve months, or a signed promise of one. That is the part that terrifies me. I have to commit to an apartment in a city I have visited once.
And the insurance?
54 euros a month for a travel and health policy that covers me until I am in the national system. It has to show a minimum coverage amount, which mine does.
Anything still missing?
Two passport photos with the correct background and my own nerve.
Approved. Four month entry visa in the passport, and I do the residence permit once I am there.
That is the big one done. What is next?
Bori. Nine years old, entirely unimpressed by any of this, and the rules for bringing a cat are stricter than the rules for bringing me.
What does she need?
Microchip first, then a rabies vaccination after the chip, then a blood titer test at least thirty days before travel, then an official health certificate issued within ten days of the flight.
Is she flying in the cabin?
Yes. The limit is eight kilos including the carrier and she is 5.4, so we are fine as long as she does not eat her feelings between now and December.
Do you want a countdown built backward from the flight date?
Please. In writing, because I will not trust myself in December.
Three apartments, all seen over video by a friend of a friend who is now owed dinner for life.
Go through them.
Graca, a one bedroom at 1,150 a month, beautiful light, sixth floor, no lift, and the stairs are the kind that turn twice.
Alvalade, a two bedroom at 1,320, quiet street, twenty minutes further out, and the second room fits a desk.
Estrela, a one bedroom at 1,400, renovated last year, the kind of place you photograph and then live in badly.
What is the deciding factor?
The desk. I work from home in a country where I know no one. If my bed and my job are in the same room I will be back in Seoul by March.
So Alvalade.
Alvalade. Twelve month lease signed, which also closes the accommodation item on the visa list.
I landed on December 20th. Bori screamed for the first hour of the flight and then slept on my feet for nine.
How is the first stretch?
Strange. Good strange. I have unpacked four boxes and I have eaten the same soup three times because it is the one thing I can order without rehearsing.
Have you started the residence permit process?
I have an appointment. March 24th. That is the earliest slot in the country and I refreshed the page for two weeks to get it.
And language?
Classes at a school called Palavra, Tuesday and Thursday evenings. They tested me and put me at A1, which is accurate and still humbling. My teacher is Marta and she does not switch to English, ever.
This week was hard. Nothing happened. That is sort of the problem.
What does hard look like on a week where nothing happened?
I spoke out loud to another human being twice on Wednesday, both times to buy something. I want my mother's kimchi and I want someone to laugh at a joke I did not have to translate first.
Is there anything close to a routine forming?
Two things. There is a Korean grocery up on Almirante Reis, tiny, run by a couple from Busan, and I go on Saturdays even when I need nothing.
And I started bouldering at a gym near the office I do not have. There is a woman named Teresa who has decided we are friends, which is exactly the right amount of aggressive.
And work across the time difference?
Brutal. Standup was landing at eleven at night my time and I was doing it in bed with the camera off.
Did you raise it?
I did. Three days a week are now fully asynchronous and I only take the live call on Tuesdays and Thursdays. It took one uncomfortable message and I waited five weeks to send it.
Residence permit done. The appointment took eleven minutes after a three month wait, which is the most bureaucratic sentence I have ever typed.
How long is the permit good for?
Two years, then a renewal. Fingerprints taken, card comes in the post in a few weeks.
Anything left hanging?
Tax. The old favorable regime for new residents closed and there is a newer one aimed at particular kinds of work, and I cannot tell from any website whether I qualify.
That sounds like a question for a person rather than a website.
Agreed. I hired an accountant, Celia, 400 euros for the first year including the annual return. She has already told me one thing I was doing wrong.
My mother is coming for three weeks in June. She has never left Asia.
What is the plan?
One week of nothing at my apartment, then Sintra for two days, then Evora, then nothing again. She will want to cook and I am going to let her fill my freezer.
How is your Portuguese holding up?
I passed A2 in April and moved to a conversation class, which is much harder and much better. I can now be misunderstood at speed.
And work?

There was a reorganization. My whole team moved under a director in Berlin named Anke, so my chain of command is now one time zone away instead of eight, which is the single best thing that has happened to my sleep.
Bori is sick. She stopped eating on Thursday and by Saturday she was hiding behind the washing machine.
Have you seen a vet?
Dr. Pinto, two streets over. Bloodwork showed her kidney values are up. Early stage, manageable, prescription food and more water and rechecks every three months.
How much was that visit?
340 euros with the bloods. I would have paid anything and he could tell, and he still charged me the normal amount, which I noticed.
How are you doing?
Fine now. On Saturday I sat on the kitchen floor and thought about what it would mean to be here without her.

I also renewed the lease for another year. And I did the arithmetic: five years of legal residence means I could apply for citizenship in 2031, which is the first time I have thought about this in years rather than months.
Well, it is settled. I am directing the Ashgrove Community Chorale, at least through the spring, which is how these things always begin.
What made it come to you?

Malcolm Ives directed it for twenty two years and he died in November, quite suddenly, and the board could not imagine a spring without a concert. I was the only person in the room who had ever held a baton.
How large is the group?
Thirty four on the roster and perhaps twenty eight who come reliably. The trouble is the tenors. There are three of them and one of them is eighty one.
Three tenors across a thirty four voice choir is thin.
It is thinner than thin. It means I cannot programme anything with a real tenor line, which rules out most of what I would like to do and most of what Malcolm left half rehearsed.
Do you want to think through repertoire that works with the voices you actually have?
Yes, and I want to do it without anyone feeling that I have written them off. This is a village, not a conservatory.
The spring programme is chosen and I feel rather pleased with myself, which is usually a sign of trouble.
What did you land on?
A movement of the Faure, which they know and can sing beautifully. A folk arrangement for the middle that lets the altos do the work. And a new piece.
A commission?

A small one. Junia Oyelaran teaches at the technical college and writes the sort of thing that sounds difficult and is not. Six hundred pounds out of the memorial fund the board set up when Malcolm died.
How did the board take spending the memorial money?
Two of them thought it should sit in the account being solemn. I said Malcolm would have found that funny and then unbearable, and they voted for it.
What has she written?
Seven minutes, four parts, and a tenor line that three men can carry without heroics. She asked me what I had and wrote for it, which is the whole art of it.
I am having the cataract done on the right eye on the 22nd. It has been like looking through a dirty window for a year and I have been pretending otherwise.
How long are you out of action?
No driving for at least a week and possibly two, and no lifting, and I am not to bend over the garden, which is April, so that is a cruelty.
Does that hit the rehearsal schedule?

It hits three Tuesdays. Wendell, our accompanist, will take those rehearsals. He has played for the chorale for nineteen years and knows the pieces better than I do, he simply does not enjoy standing up in front.
And getting to the hospital?
Ellery next door is driving me and collecting me and has already announced she is making soup, which I have not the heart to refuse.
Is the concert still comfortable timing wise?
May 17th, so yes, provided the eye behaves. I shall be back for the last four rehearsals, which is when the real work happens anyway.
We did it. I have been awake since four in the morning going over it and I want to write it down before it goes soft.
How was it received?
There were 210 people in the hall, which for a chorale that fifteen people came to hear last year is remarkable. We put chairs down the side aisle.
And the new piece?
The Oyelaran landed. There was that particular silence after the last chord where nobody wants to be the first to clap, and Junia was sitting in the fourth row looking at her shoes.
Anything that did not go to plan?
The Faure was under tempo. That is mine, entirely. I got frightened in the second phrase and never took it back.
And Dot fainted in the second half, straight backward off the riser. She is perfectly fine, she had not eaten since breakfast, but I aged a decade in the four seconds before she opened her eyes.
The tomatoes have blossom end rot again, every one on the two plants nearest the wall.
That is usually watering rather than feeding.
It is me letting them dry out and then drowning them, which I do every year and every year I am surprised.
What else is going on?
The library board has asked me to join, which I suspect means they want someone who will actually read the agenda.
And Peter is engaged. My grandson, the one who never told me anything. He rang on Sunday and said her name is Simone and they will marry next June, in Cortland, where her people are.
That is lovely news. How do you feel about it?
Very glad and slightly bruised that I heard after his mother and his brother. Which is exactly the right order and I still noticed.
The hip has become a problem I can no longer describe as a twinge. The stairs to the choir loft take me twice as long as they did in the spring.
Have you had it looked at?
Dr. Manzo took films last week. Moderate arthritis in the right hip, joint space narrowed but not gone, and he was quite firm that it is not a replacement conversation yet.
What did he suggest instead?
A cortisone injection on October 3rd and physiotherapy twice a week, which he says will do more than the injection and which I believe and resent equally.
Does it change what you can do with the chorale?
I conduct sitting on a high stool now, which I hated for one rehearsal and then found I could see the back row properly for the first time in a year.
A letter came from my brother Gordon. The first word from him in twelve years, in his handwriting, four pages.
What does it say?
It says a great deal about Tucson and the weather and very little about 2013, and then on the last page it says he thinks about our mother's house more than he expected to.
Do you want to answer it?

I do not know. He took the view that I had managed the sale to suit myself and he said so in front of the solicitor, and I have carried that sentence around for twelve years like a stone in a coat pocket.
You do not have to decide this week.
No. But he is seventy four and I am sixty eight and there is a version of waiting that is really just deciding slowly.
I answered Gordon in December. Two pages, quite short, mostly about the chorale and one paragraph about the house that took me four days to write.
Did he reply?
He telephoned on Christmas Day. We spoke for forty minutes and neither of us cried, which I count as an achievement for our family.
How did it leave things?
Unresolved and warmer. He has emphysema and he mentioned it the way one mentions the weather, at the end, on the way out of the conversation.
Are you thinking of going out there?
I am thinking about April. I have not said so to him and I have not booked anything, so it is a thought rather than a plan.
The chorale's finances have got away from us. The memorial fund is down to 1,400 pounds and we have music to buy for the autumn.
Where did it go?
The commission, the hall hire, and a piano tuning that cost more than the piano is worth.
Is there a grant route?

The Havermeyer Trust supports small music groups and the deadline is March 31st. I am applying for 5,000 pounds, which would cover two seasons of music and a proper accompanist fee for Wendell, who has been paid in biscuits for nineteen years.
I can help you draft it. What do they want to hear?
Participation and reach, which we actually have. Also, two new tenors joined in February, both under forty, and I have been dining out on it ever since.
Havermeyer came through, though not entirely. They awarded 3,500 rather than the full amount.
Does that still do what you needed?
It does one season properly instead of two, and it pays Wendell, which was the part I would not have cut.
And Tucson?
I went. Nine days in April. It was better than I had any right to expect. We did not solve 2013 and we went to a diner every morning and he showed me where he swims.
How is the hip after all that walking?
The injection wore off in March, rather sooner than Manzo predicted, and we are to have the replacement conversation properly in the autumn.
And Peter and Simone have set the date. June 20th, and they have asked me to sing, which I have not done in public since 1998.
The wedding was on Saturday and I have not stopped thinking about it since.
How did the singing go?

My hands shook and my voice did not, which is the correct order for those two things. I did an old hymn arrangement Malcolm used to trot out at funerals, which nobody there knew and everybody understood.
Was Gordon able to come?
No. His lungs and a nine hour journey do not agree. He sent a note to be read out and I read it myself, and I got through it.
What comes next for the chorale?
I am stepping back to co-director for the autumn. There is a young conductor called Ilse who has just moved into the area and has more ideas in a fortnight than I have had in a year.
I will keep the Tuesdays and she takes the programme. I am sixty nine in September and I would like to be a person who has a Saturday.
Okay so I quit my job in November and I have not told anyone how much runway is left, so I am telling you instead.
How much is left?
August. Maybe September if I stop buying coffee like a person with a salary.
And the game?
Fourteen months in. It is called Salt Lantern, you play a lighthouse keeper who can rewind ninety seconds of the world but not herself, and every puzzle is about that gap.
How much of it exists?
Three acts of five, all the core mechanics, and about forty percent of the art. It is built in Godot and I am the entire team, which is efficient right up until I get the flu.
Store page is live. It took nine days longer than it should have because I could not write the description.
How is it doing?
480 wishlists in the first two weeks, which is either fine or terrible depending on which forum post I read last.
Where did the traffic come from?
One post that did numbers and then nothing. I have no audience. I have never had an audience. I make things and then feel embarrassed about mentioning them.
The capsule art looks strong in the screenshots you sent.
That is the one thing I paid for. Pim Okada did it for seven hundred dollars and it is better than anything else on the page. Best money I have spent on this project.
A publisher called. An actual one. Fathom Row, they did that submarine game everybody liked two years ago.
What is on the table?
Thirty percent revenue share, a forty thousand dollar advance recoupable against my share, and eighteen months of console exclusivity through them.
What is your read?
Forty thousand is eight more months of being alive. That is the entire argument for, and it is a really good argument at eleven at night.
And the argument against?
Thirty percent forever for money I would spend in eight months. And the guy on the call said the word roadmap four times and never once said the word puzzle.
Fathom Row is dead. Not dramatically, just dead.
What happened?
Two things they would not move on. They wanted the game out in Q1 2026 to hit a slot in their calendar, which is nine months earlier than it can be good.
And the second?
They wanted the underwater act cut. Act four. It is the part where the rewind stops working the way you have learned and everything you know becomes a liability. It is the reason the game exists.
So you are self publishing.
I am self publishing. I said no on a Tuesday and threw up on a Wednesday and by Friday I felt better than I had in two months.
Demo is out. Puzzle Weekender runs August 18th to the 25th and I got into the main page rotation, which I did not expect.
How is it landing?
Wishlists are at 6,200 and climbing about three hundred a day while the event runs. My inbox has strangers in it.
Any problems?
One bad one. If you saved inside the lantern room the file corrupted and you lost the run. It took me until day three to reproduce it and it was a race condition in my own autosave, obviously.
Did people forgive it?
Mostly. And a streamer called Kettlewitch played the demo for ninety minutes and solved the mirror puzzle in a way I did not design, and I have watched that clip probably forty times.
Money update, since I know you were being polite about not asking.
How does it look?
Better. I got a twelve thousand dollar arts grant from the Marrowfield Foundation. It took four hours to apply and I almost did not because I assumed it was for real artists.
That plus the runway takes you where?
Into next summer if I keep being careful. And I moved. Gave up the place downtown and took a one bedroom out in Trelle, which drops my rent from $1,450 to $890.
How is that?
Quiet in a way I am not used to. My commute to work is eleven steps and my nearest friend is a forty minute train, so I am either extremely productive or in trouble, and I cannot tell yet.
Submitted to Northlight. Sixty five dollar entry fee, results in February, and every developer I respect has shown there at some point.
What did you submit?
The demo plus a two minute video I recut eleven times. The video is the best thing I have made this year and nobody will ever see it.
Anything else moving?
Localization. I paid a translator collective called Vela nineteen hundred dollars for four languages, German, Spanish, Japanese, and Brazilian Portuguese.
How did you pick those four?
Wishlist geography, mostly. Japan is fourteen percent of my wishlists and I did not expect that at all.
Northlight said no. A form email on a Tuesday morning, which I read four times looking for a sentence that was not there.
That is a real disappointment.
It is. And then on Thursday Rooftop Games Fest took me, which is smaller and in a city I can drive to and honestly probably better for a puzzle game nobody has heard of.
So there is a date now?
April 23rd. Locked, announced, on the page, no take backs.
And pricing?
$16.99 with a fifteen percent launch discount for the first week. I went back and forth between fifteen and twenty for three weeks and then picked the number my gut had picked on day one.
It is out. It has been out for five days and I have not slept properly and I am fine.
How did the first week go?
3,100 units. About thirty nine thousand dollars gross before the platform cut and before tax, which is the number I have to keep saying to myself so I do not spend it.
And reception?
Ninety four percent positive out of 210 reviews. The negatives are mostly one act being too hard, which is act two, which I already knew.
Any fires?
Two. A crash on Steam Deck in the flooded corridor, patched on day two. And a Japanese review that listed six localization typos politely and correctly, which stung more than a bad score would have.
Two months out. 8,400 units total, and June was better than May because of one video.
Kettlewitch again?
Kettlewitch again. Full playthrough, four hundred thousand views, and I watched my sales graph do a thing I have only seen in other people's postmortems.
So what happens next?
I took a contract. Two days a week at a studio called Hollow Pine doing tools work. It is not a defeat, it is a floor under me, and it means the next thing does not have to happen in eight months.
And the next thing is?
Either a DLC act for people who want more of this, or the thing I have been sketching since March that has nothing to do with lighthouses. I know which one is smarter and I know which one I will do.
Six years in the unit next month. I think I have to do the nurse practitioner thing or stop pretending I am going to.
What are you looking at?
Two programs. The state university does acute care as an online hybrid, two and a half years, about thirty eight thousand total. The private one is two years and seventy one thousand.
What does the private one buy for the extra thirty three thousand?
Six months and a placement office. That is the honest answer. Everyone says the placement office matters and nobody can tell me exactly how.
What is the pull toward doing it at all?
I am good at the bedside and my back is already forty. And I am tired of being the person who knows what is wrong and has to phrase it as a question.
Talked to Charlene about the tuition benefit. It is real but it is smaller than the rumor.
What are the terms?
$5,250 a year, which is the tax free maximum, and I owe them two years of service after I finish or I pay it back pro rata.
Is two years a problem?
Not really. I like the unit. I just do not like signing something that assumes I will.
What is left before the deadline?
March 15th. Two references and a personal statement, and Charlene said yes to writing one before I finished the sentence, which nearly undid me in the middle of a hallway.
Who is the second reference?
An intensivist I have worked nights with for four years. He will say yes and he will submit it at 11:58 on the deadline.
I got into the state program. Starts in August.
Congratulations. How does it feel?
Small, honestly. It has been a bad week and it landed in the middle of it.
What happened?
We lost a twenty four year old on Saturday. Motorcycle. He was in the unit for nine days and I had him for six of them and I knew his mother's coffee order.
I am sorry.
The debrief was ten minutes in a room with no windows and then we all went back out on the floor. That is the part I cannot get past. Ten minutes.
Anyway. August. I am also moving off straight nights to a mix, because I cannot do patho at eight in the morning after a twelve.
My father had a stroke in Kumasi on May 3rd. I flew out on the 6th and stayed three weeks.
How is he now?
Home. Left side is weak, speech is mostly back, and he is furious about the walker, which my sister says is a good sign.
Who is managing the day to day?
Adjoa. She lives twenty minutes away and she has taken all of it, and she has three children and a job. I am the one who left.
Is there a way to carry some of it from here?
Money, mostly. I am sending four hundred a month for the caregiver, which is real for me and not enough for what she is doing.
Have you told her that?
I have said thank you. I have not said the other thing. We are not a family that says the other thing.
School started August 18th. Three courses, and advanced pathophysiology is going to be the one that decides everything.
How are you scheduling it?
Patho is Tuesdays live, the other two are asynchronous. I dropped to 0.75 at work, so 24 hours instead of 36.
Does that keep your benefits?
Yes, the cutoff is 0.6, which I checked three times. The pay drop is about nine hundred a month and I have already felt it.
How is the first week?
I read the same paragraph on acid base four times on Sunday and then I got to work and explained acid base to a new grad from memory. My brain works fine. It does not work at a desk.
Four codes in seven days. Two of them mine. I do not remember driving home on Thursday.
That is a lot in one week for anyone.

It is. And in the middle of it I caught something. A heparin drip hung at the wrong concentration, the bag was right and the pump library entry was wrong, and I caught it at handoff because the number looked odd to me.
Did you report it?
I filed it. Nobody was harmed, and pharmacy found two other bags in the building within the hour.
How did the unit respond?
Well, actually. Nobody asked me who hung it. That is the part I am proud of and the part I am shaken by, because I keep thinking about the version where I was tired and the number did not look odd.
Also I got a 91 in patho, which I found out in the parking garage and did not tell anyone.
I am moving. Signed on a place on Farrow Street, two miles from the hospital.
What is the trade?
Rent goes from $1,320 to $1,590. But the commute goes from forty minutes to twelve, and forty minutes twice a day is five hours a week I am spending on a road I hate.
Does the math work on the pay you dropped?
Barely. It works if I do not eat out, and it works much better if you count the two shifts a month I will not call in exhausted for.
When is the move?
February 1st. Ridgeley has been home for five years and I will miss the tree outside the bedroom window and absolutely nothing else.
My clinical placement fell through six weeks before it starts.
What happened?
Dr. Iyengar retired. He was my preceptor, he had signed the paperwork in October, and he sold the practice and retired in March.
What is the school doing?
Apologizing. There are eleven of us in the same cohort and four are unplaced, and the placement coordinator has a spreadsheet and no leverage.
So what did you do?
Found my own. A rural clinic out in Deerhurst, fifty five minutes each way, and the doctor there said yes on a phone call that lasted four minutes.
Fifty five minutes each way is real.
It is. It is also going to be the best rotation in my cohort, because I will be the only learner in the building instead of the fourth.
My father died on April 11th. I flew back on the 12th and the funeral was on the 19th.
I am so sorry, Amina.
Thank you. It was a second stroke and it was fast and Adjoa was there, which matters more to me than I can explain.
How much time did you take?
Two weeks bereavement, three days of which the policy actually covers, and the rest unpaid. I have been back on the floor since the 4th.
And school?
Incompletes in two courses. I have until July 15th to finish both, which my advisor arranged in one email without me having to ask twice.
How are you actually doing?
I am functioning. I cried in the medication room on Tuesday because the pump alarm sounded like his phone. That is the shape of it right now.
Both incompletes are done. Finished the second one July 9th, six days before the deadline.
That is a real thing to have done in that quarter.
It is. I am back on my reduced schedule at work and I am sleeping, mostly.
Anything changing at work?
Charlene offered me charge. I said no, which surprised her and did not surprise me. Charge is a job about the floor and I am trying to leave the floor.
How does the finish line look from here?
December 2027 if I do not lose another term. Two more clinical blocks, the capstone, and boards in the spring after.
I told Adjoa the date on the phone last week. She said she is coming, which means she is coming.
I bought a boat. I want that on the record before I start explaining myself.
Go ahead and explain.
1974 Wilder 30, sloop rigged, sitting on a cradle in a field outside Munsey for four years. Six thousand five hundred dollars and the owner threw in a trailer full of hardware he could not identify.
What condition is she in?

Hull is sound where I could sound it. Deck is solid except around the mast. The engine turns about ten degrees and then stops, which means seized. The sails are the original 1974 sails and they have the texture of a paper bag.
Does she have a name?
Perpetua. Painted on the transom in gold leaf that somebody did properly, which is half of why I bought her.
What is the plan?
Two winters of work and in the water by spring after next. Roz has heard this timeline and has expressed doubt in the form of silence.
Pressure washed the bottom and I have blisters. Not on my hands.
How bad?
I counted 214 before I stopped counting. Mostly below the waterline on the port side, dime sized, and they weep when you open them.
What are the options?

The yard will peel it, dry it, and put on a full epoxy barrier coat for $9,400. Or I grind them out myself, let it dry through the summer, and roll the barrier coat, which is about $1,800 in material and six weekends.
What is the risk on the DIY version?
That I do not get the moisture down before I coat it and I seal water inside the laminate, which is how you turn six weekends into a new boat.
Which way are you leaning?
Myself, with a moisture meter and a lot of patience. Nine thousand dollars is the entire engine budget and then some.
Engine decision. I have three quotes and three opinions.
Lay them out.
Rebuild the original two cylinder diesel. Hoyt will do it for $3,800 including the injectors and a new heat exchanger, and he has done nine of them.
Repower with a new twenty horse diesel, $11,500 installed, plus a new engine bed because nothing lines up.
Or go electric, about $9,000 with the batteries, and accept that I have four hours of motoring and no heat.
What does the boat actually need to do?
Get out of a mooring field and back into it, and push through a foul tide for two hours. That is ninety percent of the job.
Then the rebuild covers it.
The rebuild covers it. Hoyt has it on his bench in August and I am the one pulling it out, which I have never done and have watched eleven videos about.
Sails. This is the part where the money goes quietly instead of loudly.
What did you price?
A new main from the loft in Cadwell is $2,300 and a new 110 jib is another $1,900. That is more than I paid for the boat.
Is used a real option on a boat this size?
It is, because a Wilder 30 has the same rig as about four other boats from that era. The loft keeps a rack of takeoffs.
What did you find?
A main off a boat that got repowered and never sailed, eleven hundred dollars, three seasons on it. And a used 110 for eight hundred that needs a new luff tape, which the loft is doing for sixty.
So nineteen hundred and change against forty two hundred.
And I get to feel superior about it every time I raise them, which is the actual return on investment.
Have to sort out where she lives next summer. The waiting lists open in November and close by Christmas.
What are the choices?
A mooring at Munsey Cove is $1,450 for the season, May to October, and you row out to it. The marina slip is $3,900 and you step off a dock with a coffee in your hand.
Which suits how you will actually use her?
The honest answer is the slip, because I will sail more if it is easy. The affordable answer is the mooring.
Is there a middle?

There is. I took the mooring and paid $220 for a dinghy rack space on the town landing, so the row is four minutes instead of a project. Twenty two hundred dollars a year saved buys a lot of engine parts.
Winter list was rewiring and a new panel. Winter list has grown.
What did you find?
The chainplates are weeping. All four, worst on the starboard forward. I pulled the first one and the bolt holes were black.
Is the core wet?
In two places. About a foot square around the starboard forward plate and a smaller patch at the port aft. I drilled test holes and got damp dust, not slurry, so it is early.
What does the repair look like?
Cut the top skin, dig out the wet balsa, dry it with a heat lamp, fill with thickened epoxy and new plywood, reglass. Three weekends and about six hundred dollars of epoxy and plywood.
And the rewiring?
Pushed to January. Which is fine. Nobody ever died of a January.
Launch date is May 9th. I have said it out loud to three people so now it is real.
What is between here and there?
Bottom paint, two gallons of ablative at $380. New through hulls and seacocks, which is the job I have been avoiding because it involves cutting holes in a boat I just fixed.
Anything from the insurance side?
That is the other thing. They will not write a policy on a fifty two year old boat without a current survey.
Have you booked one?
Marguerite Falk, $650, and she comes recommended by people who complain about everyone. She does it on the hard on April 18th, which gives me three weeks to fix whatever she finds.
She is in the water. Launched on the 9th, on schedule, which I want noted.
What did the survey turn up?

Two things I did not know about. A soft spot in the deck at the mast step, about eight inches, which I had walked over a hundred times. And the wire from the alternator to the panel is two sizes undersized, original, and had been quietly getting warm since 1974.
Both fixable?
The wire took an afternoon. The mast step is on next winter's list and she noted it as a monitor rather than a defect, which is the difference between a boat and a project.
And the first sail?

Yesterday. Eleven knots out of the southwest, full main and the used 110, and she heeled to about fifteen degrees and just sat there. I hove to and ate a sandwich and did not say anything for a while.
Then the engine overheated after twenty minutes of motoring back in and I sailed onto the mooring in front of an audience.
Halfway through the season. Fourteen days on the water so far, which is more than the last three years combined.
Did you sort the overheating?
Yes, and it was the stupidest possible thing. The raw water strainer was packed with eelgrass from the launch. Not the impeller, not the exchanger. Ten minutes and a bucket.
What is next on the ambition list?
The Sable Banks. Ninety miles, an overnight, and it is the first trip that would take me out of sight of land.
Is Roz on board with that?
Roz gets seasick in a harbor. She is genuinely happy for me and she is not coming on an overnight, and we have agreed on a coastal week in August instead, day sails and a different town every night.
August cruise is done. Six days, 140 miles, five harbors, and nobody wanted to kill anybody by the end.
How did Roz do?
She put a scopolamine patch on the night before and she was fine. Genuinely fine. She steered for two hours on the run down to Cobb Point and told me afterward she understood it now.
Any additions to the boat?
A tiller autopilot, the Tillerman 2000, $1,050 used. It steers better than I do on a long reach and it does not want to talk about anything.
When does she come out?

October 18th. And the winter job is the standing rigging, which is fifty two years old and which I have been not thinking about all season. The yard quoted $4,200 for all of it including new turnbuckles.
New year, same roadmap. I own disbursements at Northbeam and the whole year is one project whether I like it or not.
What is the project?

We are moving off Cadence, the processor we have used since the company was eleven people, onto Torrent Pay. Cadence has been end of life for two years and they keep extending it, which is the only reason we have not done it already.
What is the deadline?
End of Q3, and that is a real deadline because their contract does not renew.
Who is on it with you?
Sam Whitlock is the engineering lead. He is the calmest person in the building and he has told me twice that the timeline is fine, which from Sam means it is not fine.
What worries you most right now?
That this is a migration with no user visible benefit. Nobody gets promoted for a payout that keeps working.
Scoping is done and it is worse than the estimate, which is the most predictable sentence in my profession.
What is the volume?
220,000 payouts a month across four countries. The engineering side of that is fine, honestly. Sam has the adapters written already.
So what is the problem?
Compliance. Torrent will not onboard an account that has not been verified against their standard, and we have 18,000 dormant accounts that were verified under rules from 2019.
Meaning they have to be re-verified before they can be migrated.
Meaning exactly that. Bettina in legal walked me through it on Tuesday and I have not slept properly since. Every one of those is a real person who will get an email asking for a document.
Is there a path that does not email 18,000 people?

There is a path where we migrate the active book first and treat dormant as a separate program with its own timeline. That is what I am going to propose, and it will look like scope cutting, because it is.
Reorg. Announced Thursday at 4pm, which is when companies announce things they do not want questions about.
What changed for you?
Tom Ferrell is leaving. He hired me, he protected the roadmap for two years, and he told me on Wednesday night so I would not find out in the all hands.
Who do you report to now?
A new VP, Aditya Ranganathan, who came from a company I have heard of for reasons I will not put in writing.
What is his direction?
AI first. Everything is AI first. He asked me in our first one to one what the AI story for disbursements is and I said reliability, and he wrote something down that was not that.
Does that threaten the migration?
It does not threaten it, it starves it. It is still on the plan, it is just no longer the thing anybody senior talks about. Which is fine until I need a headcount.
Phase one shipped. Thirty percent of traffic on Torrent as of Monday.
How did it go?
Badly for four days and then fine. Error rate went from 0.4 percent to 2.1 percent within two hours of the ramp.
What was the cause?
A timeout configured at three seconds on our side against a processor whose p99 is closer to five. So we were failing perfectly good payouts and retrying them into a duplicate check.
What did you do?
Rolled back to ten percent within the hour, fixed the config, sat at ten for two days watching it, and went back to thirty on Friday. Four days total.
How did that land upstairs?
Aditya asked whether we should pause. Sam said no in a tone I have never heard him use and that was the end of the conversation.
I put my promotion case in and it came back as next cycle.
What was the stated reason?
That I need a scoped artifact that demonstrates strategic ownership. Which is a sentence, not a reason.
Did you push on what would count?
I did. He said the migration is execution, not strategy. I have moved 220,000 payouts a month onto new rails without a single customer noticing and that is execution.
Who else went up this cycle?
Wes got it. Wes shipped a dashboard redesign and presented it three times, and I do not mean that as an insult, because presenting it three times is the part I did not do.
That sounds like a lesson you are drawing rather than a complaint.
Both. I am allowed both for one more week and then I have to decide what to do about it.
It is done. One hundred percent cut over as of September 29th, and the old contract is closed for good.
Congratulations. What is the headline number?
$1.1 million a year in processor fees, which is the number I have been repeating in every room I walk into.
How clean was it in the end?
Three incidents across nine months. The worst was 47 minutes of delayed payouts in August because of a certificate nobody owned.
Did you write the postmortem?

I wrote it and I made it boring on purpose. The dormant account program is still open and I have handed it to a PM who joined in July, with everything documented, which is the most generous thing I have done all year.
A recruiter got through to me and I let her, which tells you where my head is.
What is the role?
Group PM at Halyard. Series B, payments infrastructure, about 90 people, and the hiring manager was a founding engineer at a company whose docs I have read for fun.
What are the numbers?
$215,000 base plus 0.35 percent equity over four years. I am at $178,000 with a refresh grant that is worth whatever the private market says it is worth.
Is the money the driver?
No. The driver is that a Group PM at a ninety person company gets to decide things. But the money makes the argument out loud, which is convenient.
What is the risk?
Series B. Eighteen months of runway is a rumor until it is a layoff, and I have watched three friends learn that.
I stayed. I want to walk through why, because I have told four people four different versions.
What did Northbeam come back with?

Senior PM title effective immediately, $198,000, and a retention grant vesting over three years. Aditya wrote the promotion criteria into a document with dates in it, which is the part I actually wanted.
How did the counter come about?
I told him I had an offer on a Monday and had a number by Thursday, which tells you what the last eight months of asking politely were worth.
Any regret?
Some. Halyard would have been the harder thing and I chose the known thing with a document. I am at peace with about seventy percent of that.
My area grew. Fraud and risk now sit with disbursements, which makes sense on an org chart and is terrifying in practice.
How is it going?
We had a bad one on the 14th. A rules engine change went out at 9am and by 10 it had blocked 900 legitimate payouts, mostly small merchants, mostly people who needed the money that day.
What was the fix?
Reverted in fifty minutes, released the queue by noon, and every one of them landed the same day. The damage was trust, not money.
How did you handle it?

I wrote it up under my own name and presented it at the review with my face on the slide. Sam told me afterward I did not have to take all of it, and I said the PM approved the risk threshold, so yes I did.
Aditya is gone. Eleven months, which is about what everyone predicted in the kitchen.
What happens to your group?
They have asked me to lead the payments PM group on an interim basis. Four PMs, including the one I handed the dormant program to.
Do you want it permanently?
That is the actual question and I do not know. I like the part where I decide things. I do not like that the four calendar days I spent on strategy last month were all in meetings about calendars.
How are you working it out?
I hired a coach. Fenella, $250 a session, every other week. My first session she asked what I would do with a year nobody was watching and I did not have an answer, which was the answer.
Both packages went in on Saturday. I have named the hives Curie and Hodgkin, which my students will find out about eventually and never let go.
Where did the bees come from?
A supplier out in Wexford. Italians, three pound packages with mated queens, and the drive back was two hours of forty thousand insects being extremely present in my car.
How are they settling?
Both queens released within four days. Curie is drawing comb faster, which I think is a slightly larger cluster rather than anything meaningful.
Are you feeding?
One to one syrup until they stop taking it. Which is the part I actually enjoy, standing there at seven in the evening watching them work out where the front door is.
Is this a hobby or a project?
It is a chemistry teacher with a spring free of coursework. Ask me in August.
Curie swarmed on Sunday. I did an inspection on the 14th, saw two capped queen cells, told myself I would deal with it at the weekend, and they left on the 18th.
Did you lose them?
No, and this is the part I will be telling at parties for years. They landed twelve feet up in the neighbor's pear tree in a clump the size of a rugby ball.
How did you get them down?
Borrowed ladder, a nuc box held under them with one hand, and a sharp shake. Most of them went in on the first go and the rest walked in over twenty minutes once they smelled the queen.
So you have three colonies now.
Three. The new one is Franklin. My neighbor came out mid operation, watched for a while, and asked whether this happens often, and I said absolutely not, which I hope is true.
Did alcohol washes on all three today and Hodgkin is in trouble.
What are the counts?
Curie at 2 per hundred bees, Franklin at 1, and Hodgkin at 9. The treatment threshold everyone uses is 3.
Why would one hive be so different?
Hodgkin has been the weaker colony since April, and weak colonies get robbed, and robbing brings mites home. It is also the hive I have inspected least because it is the least fun to open.
What is the treatment?
Formic acid pads, one application, fourteen days, and it works with honey supers on, which matters at the end of June.
Any risk?
Queen loss if it gets hot. The forecast is eight days of mid twenties and I am doing it anyway, because 9 mites per hundred in June is a colony that will not see February.
Harvest done. 96 pounds total across the three hives.
How did it split?
