Curie gave 48, Franklin 32, and Hodgkin 16. Hodgkin never really recovered from the treatment, which I expected and still find annoying.
How did you extract?
In the garage with a borrowed four frame extractor from Verna at the club. It took nine hours, three of which were cleaning, and my garage floor will be tacky until Christmas.
What does 96 pounds look like in jars?
About 130 jars once I have skimmed and settled it. Which is far more honey than one household can eat, which is how people end up at farmers markets.
Did the Dunmore market for the first time on Saturday. Table fee is $35 a week and you have to commit to a month.
How did you price it?
$12 for the eight ounce jar and $20 for the sixteen. I agonized over this for a week and then the woman selling goat cheese next to me told me I was underpricing and I raised it on the spot.
How did it go?
Sold out. Forty four jars in three hours and then I stood there for the last hour with an empty table feeling like an idiot and a genius at the same time.
Will you keep going?
Through October. Bringing thirty jars a week and a comb frame in a display case, because half the conversations start with someone asking what that is.
I have a neighbor problem. The Selvaggios two doors down say my bees are in their pool.
Are they?
Almost certainly. Bees need water and a pool is a warm reliable water source, and mine are the only hives within half a mile.
Is there an ordinance?

There is not, which I checked before I said a single word to anybody. The town has nothing on beekeeping at all. The health officer came out, looked at the hives, and told me privately that he keeps bees himself.
How are you handling it?
Two ways. I built a six foot lattice screen along that side of the yard, which forces the flight path up over their fence rather than across the pool.
And I put a water station with cork floats in my own yard, twenty feet from the hives, which is what I should have done in April.
And the relationship?
I brought them four jars and apologized without arguing, which cost me nothing and bought a decade of peace. My wife suggested it. I was going to bring the ordinance printout.
Lost Hodgkin. Opened it on Sunday because there was no activity on the warm day last week and the cluster was dead on empty frames.
Starvation?

Isolation starvation. There were eleven pounds of capped honey in that hive, two inches to the side of the cluster. It got down to minus eighteen for nine days and they would not break cluster to move sideways.
Could you have prevented it?

Yes. A sugar block on the top bars in December costs three dollars and takes four minutes. I did it for the other two and skipped Hodgkin because it was the weak one and I had half decided it would not make it, which is a sentence I am going to think about for a while.
How are the other two?

Curie and Franklin are both alive and flying on warm days. I ordered a nuc from Ida Prentice, a breeder two towns over, $185, ready for pickup mid April. Local stock, overwintered here, which is what I should have started with.
The school said yes to a beekeeping club. Eleven students signed up in two days, which is nine more than my chemistry club has ever had.
What does the school require?
A written risk assessment covering stings, allergies, and the walk to the hives. Epinephrine on site whenever the club meets, and the nurse trained me on it herself.
Any resistance?
One parent, and a fair objection. Her son has a severe allergy to wasp venom and she wants to know why the club is even allowed to exist.
How did you answer?
I invited her to come to the first three sessions, which are all indoors and have no bees in them at all. She is coming to the first one. That is the whole of what I can do.
Spring inspections. Franklin superseded its queen over the winter and I did not notice until I saw the new marking pattern in the brood.
Is the new queen laying well?
Beautifully. Solid frames, wall to wall, better than the queen she replaced. The bees knew something I did not, which is the story of this hobby.
And the nuc?
Installed on April 18th and it is already on its second box. Ida's stock is noticeably calmer than the packages were.
How is the club going?

Better than I hoped. A kid named Oscar spotted a queen cell in the second visit, before I did, from over my shoulder. He has read the whole book and he corrects me, and he is right about half the time.
Second harvest. 141 pounds this year across three hives, which is nearly half again on last year.
What accounts for the difference?
Three healthy colonies instead of two and a half, mite counts under control all spring, and a wet May that made the clover ridiculous.
Anything new on the selling side?
Creamed honey. I whipped forty pounds of it with a seed batch and it sells faster than the liquid at the same price, mostly to people who tell me they do not like honey.
Is the market still worth it?

The table fee goes to $45 in September, which changes the arithmetic but not the answer. And the club has asked me to teach a beginners course, six sessions, $300, which I would honestly do for free and will not say so.
Audition season. Two that matter and I have been awake since four thinking about both of them.
Which ones?
Tessera on February 20th, which is the one everyone wants, and Ombra on March 8th, which is the one I actually want.
What is the difference for you?
Tessera is beautiful and enormous and I would be a body in the back for three years. Ombra is nine people and they make things that are strange and I would be seen.
How is the rest of life holding up around this?
I open the cafe at five, I am done at eleven, I train from twelve until six. Rent is 680 split three ways with Camille and Idris, and my share is the only reason any of this is possible.
That is a lot of hours.
It is a normal amount of hours for what I am. Everyone I know does this. That is either comforting or the worst part.
Results. Tessera cut me in round two of four. Ombra called me back.
How did the Tessera cut feel?
Clean, actually. They cut sixty people in that round and the ones who stayed were all taller and all faster and I could see it from where I was standing.
And Ombra?
Ombra kept me for the full day and then asked me to come back on the 22nd for their apprentice group. There were four of us left in the room at six in the evening.
What are you working on before then?
Floorwork. Helene watched my audition video and said my standing work is ready and my floor is a tourist. She said it kindly. It was not kind.
Ombra offered me the apprenticeship.
Congratulations. What are the terms?
Nine months from September, 900 a month, company class every day and I am in the room for every creation even if I am not in the piece.
Does 900 cover your life?
Not close. Rent alone is a third of it. I keep the cafe and I move to weekends and evenings, which means I am working seven days from September.
Is there a version where you say no?
There is no version where I say no. I said yes in the room before I had done any arithmetic and I would do it again.
I rolled my ankle in class on May 30th. Landed from a jump onto the outside of my foot and heard it.
What is the diagnosis?
Grade two lateral sprain. The ligament on the outside is partially torn, not through, and there is no fracture, which is the only good sentence in the whole story.
What is the timeline?
Six weeks before full class. Tibo is my physio and he has done four dancers this year and he says the six weeks is not negotiable and the twelve weeks after that are where people ruin themselves.
September is thirteen weeks away.
Yes. I have done that arithmetic every night since the 30th. If I am not in company class on day one they will be kind about it and I will be an apprentice who arrived injured.
Back in class at about seventy percent. Full barre, marking the jumps, no landings on the left.
How does the ankle feel?
Thick. Not painful. It feels like a joint that is thinking about it, which Tibo says is normal and which I do not enjoy.
What else is happening?
I am applying for the Vlot Residency in Ghent. Three weeks in January, 1,200 euros plus housing and a studio to yourself for the whole time.
What would you make?
A solo. I have been carrying an idea about holding on to an edge for two years and I have never had three weeks and a room.
When is it due?
August 31st. Video, a page about the work, and a budget, and the budget is the part that makes me want to lie down.
Three weeks in. Company class at 9:30 every morning and I have not been late once, which for me is a personality change.
How is the ankle holding?
It holds. I tape it for anything with jumps and I take it off at night and it is fine.
And the work?

Bram is making a new piece called Undertow and it premieres at the end of the year. He is exact in a way I have never been around. He stopped me eleven times in one phrase on Tuesday and the twelfth time it was right and he just nodded and moved on.
Is that hard to take?
It is the best thing that has ever happened to me. Nobody has ever cared enough about my work to stop me eleven times.
I quit the five in the morning shift at the cafe and moved to weekends. I sleep now, which is new.
We ran Undertow at the Steen on the 14th, 15th and 16th. Three shows, all of them full.
How did it go?
The first night I could not feel my hands in the wings. The second night I danced it. The third night I understood it, which is apparently how this works and nobody tells you.
Any response?

A review in one of the Flemish papers that named me. One sentence about the solo in the third section and it used the word unhurried, which is the last word anyone would have used about me two years ago.
How did you take it?
I read it in the bathroom at the theatre and cried for four minutes and then washed my face and went to the party. Relief, mostly. Not pride. Relief.
Back from Ghent. Three weeks, started January 6th, and I have made the only thing I have ever made alone.
Tell me about it.
Twelve minutes. It is called Ledge. One performer, one light, and a floor that I have finally stopped being a tourist on.
How was working alone for three weeks?
Terrifying for six days and then the best thing in the world. Days seven through nine I did nothing but lie on the floor and I stopped panicking about that around day eight.
How is everything else?

Nils and I ended in December. Two years. It was not dramatic and it was not mutual, whatever I say to people. He said he was tired of being the person who waits at the theatre, and he was not wrong, and that is the part I keep chewing on.
Ombra has made me an offer for next season and I have two weeks to answer.
What is it?

A half contract. Ten months at 1,400 a month, which is not a living but it is a real one. The alternative is I audition in the spring and go somewhere as a full company member and start again at the bottom of a different room.
What does your gut say?
My gut says stay and my gut also says I am twenty five in August and half contracts have a way of lasting three years.
Anything else in the mix?
My right knee has been talking since February. Nothing structural, Tibo says patellar tendon, load management, but it is on the list.
And I moved. A studio on my own, 740, which is more than my old share and I have not lived alone since I was eighteen and I need it.
I took the half contract. Signed in April and I have stopped second guessing it, mostly.
What made the decision?
Bram, honestly. He asked what I wanted to make and then asked again a week later, which nobody in a big company would ever do.
What is happening with the solo?
Ledge is programmed at a small festival in Liege in September. Twenty minutes of stage time, a 600 euro fee, and my name on a poster that I did not have to design.
And money generally?
Better. I teach a beginners class on Saturday mornings for 90 a week, twelve adults who have never danced and who are more fun than anyone in my professional life.
How is the knee?
Managed. Tibo gave me a loading program and I have done it almost every day, which for me is a miracle of character.
Thirty three years at Renner Tool and Die in March. They sent the pension estimate and I have read it four times and I want somebody to check my thinking.
What are the options?
Single life is $2,410 a month and it stops the day I do. Joint and 75 percent survivor is $2,180 a month and Deb keeps three quarters of it if I go first.
What does Deb have of her own?

A 401k from the school district with about ninety thousand in it and she is fifty eight. That is it. She was home with the kids for eleven years and that shows up right here, on this page, thirty years later.
Two hundred thirty dollars a month is the price of the insurance, effectively.
That is how I have been looking at it too. Twenty three hundred a year for her to not be poor if I drop dead at sixty five.
Is there a deadline on the election?
Not yet. But I would rather decide it in my kitchen than in an office with a folder in front of me.
There is a rumor going around the shop that they are killing second shift. Third time in five years so nobody is panicking, but this one has a date attached to it.
Are you on days?
Days for eleven years. If second goes I am fine. If second goes it also tells you what they think of the whole plant.
Are you doing anything about it?
I have started pricing what retirement actually looks like, which turns out to mean I have started pricing recreational vehicles.
What is on the list?

A used 2018 Class C, twenty six feet, one owner, $58,000 and it drives like a truck because it is one. Or a travel trailer at $24,000, which is cheap until you notice I do not own anything that can pull it.
So the trailer is really a trailer plus a truck.
Which is $24,000 plus another twenty and a hitch. Deb says do not buy anything with wheels until you know what your Tuesdays look like, and she is right and I hate it.
Went in for the physical the plant makes us do and came out with a diagnosis.
What did they find?
Type two diabetes. A1c came back at 8.1, which Priest tells me is not borderline, it is a number you act on. He put me on metformin, 500 twice a day, and told me to walk after dinner.
How are you taking it?
Badly for a day and then fine. My father had it and lost two toes and did not change a single thing he ate. I would rather not do that.
What is changing at home?
Deb reorganized the whole kitchen inside a week. There is no white bread in my house anymore. I have been informed that we are a household that eats beans now.
Are you walking?
Forty minutes after dinner most nights. It is the only part of this I actually like, which I am not going to tell her.
Not a rumor anymore. They announced the whole plant closes in March of next year.
The whole plant.
All of it. 118 people. The work goes to two plants down south and the equipment goes with it, some of which I have run since 1994.
What is the severance?
Two weeks of pay for every year of service. That is the formula and they read it off a card in a room with no chairs.
How did people take it?

Quiet. A couple of the young guys were angry, which is right. The rest of us have been waiting for this since the last owner sold. I went back out and finished the run because the parts were already in the machine.
I have decided. I am not looking for another shop. I am retiring when the doors close.
What decided it?

I priced myself. There are three shops within an hour that would hire me tomorrow, and every one of them would want me on nights to start, at four dollars an hour less, running machines I would have to learn.
And you are sixty one.
Sixty two in November. If I work three more years at a place I do not like I will not get those three years back and I will still be retiring.
What about the pension paperwork?
The election has to be in sixty days before my last day, and human resources says once it is in it cannot be changed. That is the sentence they say twice.
Have you and Deb settled it?
We have talked about it four times and stopped in the same place each time. It is not the number. It is that picking one means saying out loud which one of us goes first.
Went back to Priest for the three month bloods. A1c is 6.4.
That is a large move in five months.
Nineteen pounds off and the walking and Deb's beans. He said if it holds through the winter we talk about backing off the metformin, which I did not know was on the table.
Anything else new?
I bought the motorhome. The 2018 Class C, twenty six feet.
What did you pay in the end?
$52,000. It sat on their lot all summer and I went back in October with a number and a check and did not say much, which is a thing my father taught me and which works about half the time.
Where is it now?
In the side yard under a cover, which Deb says looks like a beached whale. She has already picked out where the coffee pot goes.
Renata called and asked for money. Fourteen thousand dollars, and she had a spreadsheet, which tells you she was expecting a fight.
What is it for?
She has been a dental hygienist for nine years and the practice she is at is selling shares to the staff. Fourteen thousand buys her a piece and a seat at the table.
Is it a good deal?
I looked at the numbers she brought and it is not a bad one. The practice is busy and the dentist is fifty and not going anywhere.
What does Deb think?
Deb says no. Not because of the money but because Renata has come to us three times in ten years and it is always a spreadsheet. She thinks I say yes because I like being asked.
Where did you land?
Eight thousand, and I told her it is a gift, not a loan. That way nobody owes anybody at Christmas for the next five years. Deb has not said much about it, which is how I know we are not done.
Last day is March 6th. It is on a piece of paper on the refrigerator, which Deb put there.
How is the severance shaking out?
There is a cap nobody mentioned in June. Twenty six weeks maximum, no matter your service. On the formula I would have had sixty six weeks. I am getting twenty six.
That is a substantial difference.

It is forty weeks of pay. A couple of the older guys are talking to a lawyer. I read the plan document and the cap has been in there since 2011, so I think we are talking to a lawyer about our own reading comprehension.
What about health coverage?

Three options and only one of them is sane. Continuation coverage is expensive, the marketplace is a maze, and Deb's district plan will take me as a spouse for $310 a month. That is the answer and it took two nights to be sure of it.
Retired. March 6th, walked out at 3:30 with a box and a cake nobody ate.
How is it sitting with you?
Strange. I have woken at 4:40 every single day for thirty three years and my body has not been told.
Did the pension get sorted?
It did. Joint and 75 percent survivor, $2,180 a month, filed in January. Deb cried at the kitchen table and then made me sign it before either of us could think about it any more.
And Social Security?
Deferring to sixty seven. The severance and the pension carry us and the difference between sixty two and sixty seven is real money for the rest of it.
What is next?

Three weeks in the motorhome in May, out to Copper Gorge and back. And we have started talking about selling the house. Four bedrooms for two people and a set of stairs I do not need at seventy five. Deb's hometown is Alder and there are ranch houses there for half of what we would get.
Back from the trip. Three weeks, 2,100 miles, and I would do it again tomorrow.
Any trouble?
The alternator went outside a town called Tybee Springs on a Sunday. $740 and a day and a half, and the guy who did it had a Bridgeport in the back of his shop that was older than me.
How is retirement treating you otherwise?
This is the part I did not expect. I was bored by the middle of June. Genuinely bored. There are only so many things in a house that need fixing and I fixed all of them by Memorial Day.
What did you do about it?

Took a job. Two days a week at Dunbar Machine, twenty minutes away, $32 an hour and I pick the days. No nights, no quotas, and I told them up front I will not be there in the last two weeks of May because we will be somewhere else.
And the house?
We had an agent walk through in June. She said we would get more than I thought. I have not agreed to anything and Deb has already been looking at Alder listings on her phone at breakfast.
We got hit properly last Thursday. A credential harvesting campaign dressed up as a payroll notice, sent to 230 mailboxes.
What was the damage?
41 people opened it and 9 typed their password into the fake page. Two of those had access to a scheduling system with patient names in it.
How did you find out?
A nurse manager forwarded it to us with the words this looks fake, which is both the best and the worst thing about our detection posture.
Is multifactor in place?
Not on webmail. That is the whole story. We have three people in security for a 4,200 person organization and I have been asking for multifactor since I got here.
Does this change the conversation?

It might. Grant Osei is our chief information security officer and he is a contractor, three days a week, which means he can say the uncomfortable thing without worrying about his career. I am going to ask him to say it.
Multifactor is approved. All 4,200 staff, funded, with a project manager, which I did not ask for and now cannot imagine doing without.
How are you sequencing it?
Pilot first with our own department and finance, about 180 users, because if it breaks I want it breaking on people who can walk to my desk.
What about shared clinical workstations?
That is the hard part. You cannot ask a nurse to pull out a phone forty times a shift. We are buying 300 hardware keys, the Vellum ones, at $28 each, which live on the badge lanyard.
Any resistance so far?
A group of surgeons has already written to the chief medical officer. The letter uses the phrase patient care delays four times in two paragraphs.
Do you have a baseline to argue from?
We ran our own simulated phish two weeks ago before anything changed. 18 percent click rate across the organization. That number is now on the first slide of every deck I will make this year.
A hospital two counties over got encrypted last week. Ambulances diverted for four days, and they went back to paper charting.
Are you exposed the same way?
That is what I spent Tuesday finding out. We ran a tabletop with the executive team, four hours, and the scenario was deliberately unfair.
What broke in the exercise?

Backups. We keep 30 days of retention and every copy is reachable from the same domain the servers are on. If someone gets domain admin they get the backups too, and I have been saying that in writing for a year and a half.
Did the exercise move anything?
It did, and I hate that it took someone else's disaster. The chief financial officer approved immutable backup storage at $46,000 a year, in the room, before the tabletop was even finished.
What was the moment that did it?
I asked how long the organization could run on paper. Nobody answered. The silence was worth more than the eleven memos.
Rollout is at 62 percent of staff. The easy 62.
What is holding the rest?
Exceptions. We are carrying 240 of them and the list grows every week, because every exception is signed off by someone senior who is annoyed.
Is there a policy problem underneath that?
There is. We wrote the policy assuming a person at a desk. Clinical work is a person moving between eleven workstations in an hour, and the policy makes them authenticate at each one.
Who is pushing back hardest?
Dr. Lourdes Camara, the chief medical officer. She is not wrong and she is extremely difficult to move, which is a bad combination for me.
Where did you land?

A compromise I can defend. Eight hour session persistence on trusted clinical workstations inside the hospital network, phone or key for everything else, and no exceptions for remote access at all. She took it in twenty minutes once I stopped arguing about principles.
External assessment came back. A firm called Brightwater did six weeks of work and gave us 14 findings.
How bad?
Three highs and I already knew all three, which is either vindicating or damning.
What are they?

Backup tapes going offsite unencrypted with a courier. A flat network in radiology where every device can talk to every other device. And service accounts whose passwords have not changed since 2017, two of which have domain admin.
What is the remediation plan?
Encryption on the tapes is done already, it took an afternoon and a setting. Service accounts are a six month project because half of them run things nobody will admit to owning.
And radiology?
Radiology is a year and a fight. Segmenting that network means touching machines that are under vendor support contracts that forbid us from touching them.
I need to talk about the on call rotation before I do something unprofessional.
What is the current state?
Rohit left in November. He gave four weeks and he was right to go. That took us from three to two, which means I am on call every other week, permanently, with no end date.
How is that landing?
I got paged at 2:40 in the morning on my daughter's birthday for a false positive from the endpoint tool. That was the moment I stopped being reasonable about it.
Did you escalate?

I wrote it up as a risk rather than a complaint. Attrition, response times, single points of failure, and what happens in an actual incident when both of us have been awake for twenty hours. Grant walked it upstairs and we have approval to hire two, not one.
Anything to reduce the noise in the meantime?
Tuning the endpoint tool. Eleven rules generated 70 percent of our alerts and eight of them were tunable in an afternoon once I sat down and actually did it.
We had a real one on Monday. Not a drill and not a false positive.
What happened?
An engineer from Corvid Imaging, one of our scanner vendors, plugged his own laptop into a wall port in radiology to run diagnostics. That laptop had been on four other hospital networks this month.
What did it bring?

An old worm, ten years old, that scans for a file sharing vulnerability we patched years ago. It found 31 devices in radiology that still have it, because those devices are under vendor contracts and cannot be patched by us.
How long to contain?
Three hours from first alert to isolated. We pulled the segment off the network and worked with the vendor engineer, who was mortified and genuinely helpful.
Any harm?

No patient impact and no data movement. And the thing I have been unable to fund for four months now has an executive sponsor, because a slide with the word worm on it does what eleven memos could not.
I passed the incident handling certification. Second attempt.
Congratulations. What happened the first time?
I sat it in January and missed by four points. Four. I had done the practical sections in my sleep and I lost it on the policy and governance domain, which I had dismissed as the easy part.
What did you change?
Studied the boring half properly, which took six weeks of evenings, and I am now the person at parties who knows about evidence handling chains.
Did the hospital cover it?
Both attempts. $1,300 each and education funds paid for the first, and Grant found the second out of a training budget that had gone unspent since 2023.
Multifactor is done. 100 percent of staff as of June 1st. Eleven months from approval to complete.
That is a real accomplishment for a three person team.
Two person for most of it. The number I actually care about is the phishing one. We ran the same simulation as the baseline last week and the click rate is 4 percent.
That is a big change.
It is, and I will not pretend the training did it. Multifactor did it. Every phish that used to be an incident is now a rejected push notification and an annoyed user.
Anything else changing?

Grant's contract ends at the end of June. They have hired a permanent chief information security officer, Deirdre Naughton, who is coming from a bank and who asked me in her interview loop what I would do with three more people.
Three weeks in with Deirdre and the whole shape of the job is changing.
What are her priorities?
Identity governance first, which means who has access to what and why, and nobody here has ever been able to answer that in one place.
And second?
Third party risk. We have 900 vendors with some form of access and the register of them is a spreadsheet that three people maintain differently.
Where does that leave you?
She offered me a lead role. Two of the new hires would report to me, plus $14,000, plus a standing seat in meetings I currently hear about afterward.
Do you want it?
I want the seat and I do not want the meetings, which is not a position anyone gets to hold. I have until the end of August.
